utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then let us have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Joanna --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also in the Defence case, the Prosecution starts in the common-law system, and it doesn't change?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it doesn't actually. It's always still the Prosecution who start. But I'm happy for the Defence to start. Your Honours, it's Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, and Ruth Karper, case manager, for the Prosecution. And on behalf of the Prosecution, I welcome Your Honours' new colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this immediately. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence. And our welcome to the new Judge as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start the Defence conference as scheduled, please let me introduce to you our new Judge. Under Rule 17, sitting now to my left-hand side, the Honourable Judge Ms. Carmen Argibay. I still have some problem but we will learn as soon as possible from Argentina. I don't want to go into more details of her vitae here and now. For those who are interested, the entire CV, is like all the CVs of Judges acting in this Tribunal accessible on the United Nations Internet website. The short version was in addition distributed to the press immediately after her solemn declaration, 4th November this year. Thereby, this Tribunal is operational again, Trial Chamber. And you will be aware that our new colleague on the Bench is already on the top of the case in a number of details, sometimes even more on the top of the case than the other Judges where it's already faded a little bit. But due to the fact that we have all the possibilities here, not only transcripts but also videos, it's extremely -- I won't say easy, but it's possible to have access to what has been said in the past in this case. So there are no, in principle, no obstacles, to restarting the case immediately. The only visible and audible change will be that the language in this case will be from now on English only. Of course, translated into the language the accused understands. No doubt, this will speed up our proceedings. And in principle, it will be no longer necessary to, for example, read out documents in open Court. This brings me immediately to the start of the pre-Defence conference. And at the same time, a short Status Conference. The parties have received the Chamber's 98 bis decision, I hope, in a language everybody understands, also when reading between the lines. One thing I have to emphasise in addition is that all the interim decisions during the Prosecution's case had been unanimous decisions. In the meantime, we received a number of motions in writing. It is for all of us to settle these disputes emanating from these motions hopefully already today. And in addition, I hope that we can continue with our practice raising issues, in principle, in open court and receiving answers and decisions orally, in principle, as well. When having before us all the motions of the last, say, ten days, the question is what has priority? To a certain extent, I was alerted by the motion of the Defence by November -- November 11, the final list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter (g). This brings me to ask as usual in the framework of a Status Conference, Dr. Stakic in person, Dr. Stakic, what about your health condition? Do you have any complaints regarding this or do you have any complaints regarding your situation in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. At the moment, I have no objections to raise concerning the conditions, and I am in good health. Thank God for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. May I then ask Defence counsel, on the list of your envisaged witnesses and experts under number 100, I found - and this was alerting me - that you're requesting a neuropsychiatrist. And therefore, my question to you, what is the background? Is this the health condition of your client, or why did you want us to hear an expert on -- I've never heard this word before, but apparently it seems to be related to the health of your client. Please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's the opposite, that we want to prove that Dr. Stakic is very normal and ready to go back to a normal life. And also, we want to refute some statements from one of the journalists who testified in front of this Court who stated that Dr. Stakic seemed to be crazy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's not related in any way to the actual health, state of health, or to the question of culpability. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's not our Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This is already a relief. Let us come back to this motion a little bit later. But I think now, priority has the latest motion filed by the Defence November 13th, a motion for mistrial. Normally potatoes are not eaten as hot as they are cooked but I can't anticipate what is behind this motion. There are several alternatives, and let -- before I give the possibility to the Prosecution for a response, one question remains open: Under (b), you mention that the Trial Chamber should enter an order to strike from the record the testimony of certain witnesses to be identified by the Defence in open court. Could you please let us know what witnesses you have in mind when making this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't identified -- we really didn't have time by now to do this, all the witnesses we had in mind. But it relates to the witnesses who testified about the issues clarified by the 68 bis disclosures, clarified by the witnesses who were questioned by the OTP in March this year, and June or July last year. And those witnesses were members of the Crisis Staff. And we didn't have a chance to see those statements, and we didn't have a chance to cross-examine the witnesses who testified on crucial issues relating to this case. First of all, we think about the politicians who took part in the political life of Prijedor Municipality in 1992, like [redacted] or Sejmenovic or Murselovic because we couldn't cross-examine them correctly at that time. Another issue relating to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't start with this. It started already with the Defence first 65 ter (g) letter, and then the additional final list of witnesses. To be honest, we can't live in this way. You can't just tell the Court that you miss certain witnesses to be identified in open court. You can't expect this Trial Chamber to search somewhere in the fork what do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Your Honour goes on, I was going to say would Mr. Lukic be kind enough not to identify these witnesses by name he's already mentioned, one who was protected. So I would ask that that be -- I'm not sure how to do this now without repeating this, but in any event before this goes out, it needs to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we please, Madam Registrar, redact the name from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Karper has written the name down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. When I say identify in open Court, of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. course I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- refer to the names but to the pseudonyms and otherwise give us access to what the Defence really wants. And that yes, let's continue. So I think as to the fact that you are not able to identify these witnesses in open court here and there, and you had enough time, no doubt enough time, to prepare the Defence case, and before coming with this accusations vis-a-vis the other party, it would be fair enough and it would be necessary to identify these persons that we are aware what you are complaining of, and then we can react in the adequate way. Because no doubt, in case there was prejudice, then we would have to discuss possible consequences. But if you mention only "witnesses" as such without going into concrete details, it's not possible for us. Under (c), you state that the Court enter an order compelling the OTP to produce the statements in full of the witnesses identified in the disclosures of 18 October, 21 October, 28 October, and 28 October once again, the second. And enter an order accepting each of the Rule 68 disclosures as being exculpatory and admit the same as evidence. Could you please go into some more details so that the Trial Chamber is able to understand what is the underlying request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, these days we are receiving almost every day the whole list of 68 bis that usually only lists. We don't receive, for example, the whole testimony. We receive only fragments, so we are also unable to check the statement of the witness, if it's only fragmental. We don't know what's the substance of the rest of the statement. And it's -- the case of the Prosecution is over. That's the manner of the work of the Prosecution in every single case. We have it in Samac case. They disclosed the bunch of the documents during the Defence case. In Krstic case, they disclosed a whole pile of documents after the appeal brief. So if we are expecting to work in this trial that way, we are not ready to proceed. We have to know what our Defence is. We cannot have our Defence before we have all the documents. Investigation is entrusted to the Prosecution, and they do the complete investigation. They have the documents. For example, we asked the Kozarski Vjesnik for issues from April and May, we received information from the OTP that they don't have it. In Kozarski Vjesnik, we were told that everything was taken by the OTP. So also, we would like to clarify that question. And if this Tribunal is not powerful enough to press and to order the Prosecution to disclose everything necessary to the Defence, we ask the Court to order the Prosecution to give that statement in front of the Dutch notary public so if it's not fulfilled, we at least have some kind of weapon against the OTP to get what we have to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the Defence doesn't need additional weapons, and we should refrain from using these terms. In case you are concrete, there's no problem, and here, in fact, save the second disclosure as of 28 October, 2002, it was disclosure 1164 ongoing, 1166, we have this before us. And as I already said earlier, this Trial Chamber being composed of Judges of civil-law systems totally dislikes this approach, that the parties present us some facts, extracts of facts, and then it's for the Judges to fish in the sea to find the additional, the complementary evidence. Therefore, I would ask the Prosecution, what are the reasons for disclosing these documents at this point in time after the end of the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I need to explain to Your Honour the processes that have gone on here, and it's going to take -- it's not an instant answer. Your Honour, however, may I start by saying this more in sorrow than in anger, that I deplore the phrases and the tone of the motion that was filed, which I have no doubt at all was written by Mr. Ostojic because it reflects very strongly the American style of advocacy, which I've become used to in the Brdjanin case and I'm sorry Mr. Ostojic is not here today to uphold the allegations and the hyperbole which is contained in this motion. Your Honours, I think the pertinent question you asked Mr. Lukic a minute ago, to identify the witnesses he says that they would have been cross-examined differently, and his inability to do so shows I regret to say that this motion is simply an attempt, as they set out in paragraph 41 of the motion, that they effectively wish to delay the start of the case. All they had to do was say that. Your Honours know that we also would have been happier if the case could have started after January, without trying to drag up allegations of misconduct by the Prosecution. Now, Your Honours, the rules state this, and can I remind Your Honours in light of some of the requests, of Rule 66, first of all, that we are obliged to disclose to the Defence copies of statements of all witnesses whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial, and all written statements taken in accordance with Rule 92 bis. Rule 66(B) entitles the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control, which are material to the preparation of the Defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial, et cetera. Now, Your Honour, a specific letter was written to the Defence in, I believe -- I had a copy of it a moment ago. January, yes, I'm sorry. The 25th of January of this year asking them whether they wished to invoke the -- their ability to inspect everything we had under Rule 66(B). We received no reply to that, though I believe verbally they said no, they were not proposing to use that rule. Your Honour, we then moved to Rule 68, which is the -- really the rule that affects this particular aspect of the case. "The Prosecutor shall as soon as practicable disclose to the Defence the existence of material known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence." Now, Your Honour, no one in this Tribunal is unaware of that, and particularly no one in the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honour, I think I've already mentioned this once to Your Honour before, but the quantity of material held by this Office in respect of Prijedor is simply enormous. It is not, I think, an exaggeration to say that over the ten years or so that this Tribunal has been in existence, or eight years, there must be hundreds and hundreds of thousands of pages of documents that in some way or another relate to Prijedor. Your Honours, as a result, from the moment that this case began, and Dr. Stakic was arrested, the Office of the Prosecutor had unceasingly engaged in searches to identify material under Rule 68. Now, because of the huge amount of material that we knew that we had, we wrote to the Defence about this on the -- Your Honour, I'm sorry I keep losing my letters. Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. In January. It was the same letter that we wrote in respect to that. We wrote asking this: "As a further matter, I would like to inform you it would greatly assist and expedite the Rule 68 searches if you could provide the Prosecution with any specific type of document that you feel will be relevant to a possible Defence in your case. Such search criteria would enable us to make more efficient use of the in-house search facilities. If you would like to discuss these matters further, please do not hesitate to contact Nicholas Koumjian." Your Honour, absolutely no response was received to that letter. Of course, the Defence are entitled to remain silent about what the nature of their Defence is or what documents they would like us to look for, but that doesn't help us. Your Honour, I had drawn up over the weekend -- I've made inquiries, and if necessary we can reduce this to a schedule for Your Honours' perusal. We employed 15 people over a period of some, adding up the total hours engaged - this is of course -- nobody actually timed it to an exact time -- the amount of time they spend in it, but this is an estimate, 2.942 man hours have been spent in looking for Rule 68 material in respect of Stakic. A total of 1.000 -- and I say a total, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this is an estimate as best we can, 167.000 documents, Your Honour, have been searched. That's documents, Your Honour, not pages. So the pages are something that we can't even begin to quantify. Your Honours, records have been kept as far as is possible of all the material searched. A lot of the material has never been translated into English, and therefore it is necessary to use language staff to try and identify what may be in that material. Now, Your Honour, the rule says "the nature of the material." Until the Trial Chamber on the 30th of October, because the same point has been raised in the Brdjanin case over Prosecutor -- as I say, this seems to be an American habit of making allegations that the Prosecution have been behaving improperly. We have understood the rule to mean it was of sufficiency to produce a summary of the Rule 68 material. It was not necessary to produce the whole statement because these people weren't being called as witnesses, and there's an extra added difficulty which I will explain to Your Honour. But Your Honour, all the letters that were sent to the Defence said this: "Please find enclosed short summaries and documents which contain resulting from ongoing searches, which contain information that may fall within the ambit of Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In the event that any of the summaries are of interest, please advise." We have never been advised that they have required any of the full statements from which the summaries have been produced. In the Brdjanin case, Mr. Ackerman quite often said he required the full statements. These were provided with redactions. And the problem has been, Your Honour, that particularly where witness statements are concerned, these witnesses were all seen over a period of years. Some of them were seen by the Bosnians. Not one of them were ever informed that they may have to be, their names, may have to be given to the Defence. And so where the Defence have either asked for the witness statement, we have taken out the names and said if you require to contact these witnesses, you must let us know because we have to let them know that their particulars and their statements are going to be provided to the Defence because they were never told that this might happen. And it would not be right in our view to do that. Your Honour, not once, not once since we have been disclosing the material to the Stakic Defence team have we ever received a request until Your Honours were asked to make this order in the motion. Your Honours, we have been disclosing since this case began Rule 68 material right from the beginning because the first searches that were done were the obvious ones on material that was exculpatory of Dr. Stakic himself. We, however, took the view that we had to go a great deal further and we must, therefore, search for documents and statements that contradicted anything that our witnesses might have said. And that, as I say, has taken a long time indeed. It has been a search carried out not just for the Stakic case but for the Brdjanin and Talic. And that is why these disclosures relating to the summaries have been coming so late. Your Honours, to suggest that we have deliberately withheld knowingly information which may assist the Defence is a disgraceful suggestion. If we were going to do that, then why didn't we sit on it completely and wait for the appeal? And what advantage is it to us not to disclose this material? Now, Your Honours, the summons material that Mr. Lukic -- the motion explains about it. Your Honours, these people were interviewed as the Defence say in March of this year. We did actually disclose what we considered to be the obvious Rule 68 material in that some time ago. For example, one of the people interviewed -- thank you very much. I do apologise. I have a lot of paper here today. On the 12th of March, we disclosed the material, for example, from one of them there was complaint made that he stated he did not believe that Stakic went to Omarska. Your Honour, as the case has gone on, it has become clearer what the Defence is, other than the obvious one that Dr. Stakic had no power. And so we've had to go back and re-look at the people who were interviewed. And Your Honour, I do regret, and it is entirely my failing, that we didn't go back and look at those interviews earlier. It simply fell through the cracks. There was so much other reviewing going on of transcripts that I forget to issue instructions to go back to those interviews and see what else could be classed potentially as Rule 68. And so that is the reason for the delay. I'm afraid I gave -- this was the complaint in the Brdjanin case as well. I gave the same explanation. It is a failure, a human failing. It was not done deliberately. As I say, we have no reason to withhold this material. But it's only disclosed in summary form because that's what the rules say, or in fact we now disclosed the actual words used as a result of the order in the Brdjanin case. And we thought having received that order, it would be wrong, even though there had been no order in this court, and although the norm is to disclose the nature, a summary, of what the material is. And that's why they have got it in this form. Your Honours, we would say that they have received all the material that they are entitled to. If Your Honour feels that they should have the whole of the summons interview, then we will turn it over. But we do say that is not something that is -- they are entitled to, and there are good reasons why they should not get it unless and until these persons are actually called by the Defence as witnesses. Because one of the matters that Your Honours will have to decide is upon the credibility of these people if they are called as Defence witnesses and if they have said something completely different to the Defence and in the witness box from what they have said to us, so that may be a matter that Your Honours wish to consider. All of these people, Your Honour, are known to the Defence. It's not that we have interviewed people that they could not have known about and have not known about. These are obvious if the Defence wished to call evidence about the Crisis Staff, these are obvious witnesses. And Your Honours may recall, we had some discussion when Your Honours were inviting us to call witnesses who were hostile to our case. Your Honours, the -- as I say, it is abundantly clear, we suggest, that all of this is simply a tactic to try and delay the start of the Defence case. And it was an unnecessary tactic because we have every sympathy for the Defence on this. We suggest that if the Defence are able to identify questions that they would have asked of witnesses who have been called which they could not have asked or would not have asked because they didn't know about this material, then we will have those witnesses recalled. But Your Honours, at the moment, judging by Mr. Lukic's inability even to name the witnesses that he says they would have questioned differently, that this is as I say nothing more than a tactic. But if they can identify the questions they wanted to ask, if those questions are proper or admissible, and they were not able to ask them because they did not have the information, then we will arrange to have these witnesses recalled. Your Honours, I'm sorry to have taken so long but I felt it was necessary to go a little bit into the history of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you for your submission. As mentioned before, I think according to the answer as regards point (b) of the request by the Defence as to the fact that the Defence is not able to identify these witnesses today, for today, this request is moot. But let us come to point (c). The request is related to, first of all, to disclosures, the 18th of October. Disclosure number 1161, and then 1162, the 21st of October, and 28 of October. We have first of all the report of the commission on the inspection of collection centres and other facilities for captives in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I think there should be no doubt among the parties that Rule 68 doesn't expire at the end of the Prosecution's case, and there is the ongoing obligation to disclose exculpatory material. Therefore, I believe there is nothing special with these brief descriptions. And I understand the Prosecution, if the Defence so want, they can have, no doubt, access to the entire documents mentioned in these brief descriptions. Are you satisfied as regards these summaries, having access to all the materials? I think Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nothing more can be granted. I come back to the 1167 when it's -- sorry, 1163 ongoing, I come back later. But now it's only on those disclosures where we have only summaries. Are you satisfied that you have access to these documents as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I first have to mention that I received those documents yesterday. Actually I found only those charts in my locker. I haven't received it before,. And the documents, witness statements, those fragmental witness statements, I got through the motion of Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that you yourself signed this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that you yourself signed this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the fact is that I haven't seen those documents before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you are prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are prepared to answer in this language we are not acquainted with in this courtroom without seeing the underlying documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to go back to the statement of Ms. Korner. She gave a long and nice speech. The problem is that we are discussing here about the members of the Crisis Staff, and if this is not the trial about the Crisis Staff, I don't know what kind of trial is this. They interviewed the members of the Crisis Staff in March this year, a few days before the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please don't confuse. I draw your attention only to the first summaries, and not to the others. I explicitly stated earlier that I'll come back to this 1163 and ongoing, the interviews on March later, because I think this is a different problem. My question is only related now to these brief descriptions of the 18th and 22nd of October. And my question was, does it suffice that you have access to these documents as stated by the OTP? Then we can come back later to the other...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to explain to me what kind of access you have in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we discussed this earlier in this case. When there is a summary, and disclosure of a Rule 66 or Rule 68 information, this means that there is a document available with the OTP. And in the beginning, I recall that the Defence agreed that it shouldn't be for the Prosecution to label a document as an exculpatory one. So therefore, it is a hint that they have found new documents. And if you so the want, you have access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will provide, so there's no misunderstanding, we will provide the full statement of the person from whom this extract was taken, but we will redact at this stage the identifying details, the name. But the statement will be there. If you require the name, because you wish to interview the witness, then if you make the request, we will contact, if we can, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are satisfied with this kind of disclosure. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The report of the commission, this was disclosure number 1167. I think you have received it in full?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then let's turn to that where we received already the apologies by the Prosecution. And no doubt that also the Trial Chamber, when being confronted with these documents, were to a certain extent surprised and disappointed not to have these documents before us and now only, if I understand it correctly, extracts. And please, could you please specify your request as regards these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like to have the full statements of the witnesses interviewed by the OTP. I don't know whether they would be protected witnesses or not, so if we are mentioning the names, it would be advisable to go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that normally one can understand a document only as a whole, when taking only parts from a document and from a statement, there is already a kind of evaluation, and I think the most appropriate way is to present the entire statements requested here, not only to the Defence but also to the Trial Chamber, that we have all the same access, the same knowledge on these crucial points, and therefore I think there is no obstacle in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is rather different. As I said, if Your Honours order it, then we'll do it. But these are people who the Defence have had the opportunity to interview themselves. And as I say, there's a real reason for us not handing over people that we are not calling that we interviewed under Prosecutor's summons who we have reason to believe, not reason to believe, who are accomplices effectively. And we would prefer that the Defence only get that to which they are entitled. But I know that Your Honour is very keen on full statements, so if Your Honour orders it, we'll hand them over. But what I do not wish this to be thought of as a precedent because this has an effect on many other cases in this building. It is not something that the Defence would be entitled to under the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, there's one other thing that Mr. Koumjian rightly reminds me of. Just before Your Honours rules, could I just mention this: There are certain persons - we're not saying these are part of them - who have actually cooperated in a sense and could be dangerous, I think, if that were discovered. I'm not saying that any of these do, but that's the principle behind nondisclosure as well of the full transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to present the entire statements to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber. May the names be, if necessary, redacted. And if there are any included, included in the statements, then we can decide later on. But first of all, it's for you to present the documents and we can discuss any redactions later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we'll do ask if we decide there are certain parts we wish to redact, we will put them before Your Honour to make a ruling under Rule 66 (c).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence is satisfied with this proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And thank you, Your Honour. Only one more thing relating to these witnesses. We want clarification from the OTP whether they asked those witnesses if they have been approached by the Defence because two of those witnesses were approached by the Defence before the OTP approached them. So first of all I would like to get the answer from Mr. Koumjian who obviously interviewed those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal with that because we asked the same question whether any of these persons have made statements to the Defence. Your Honour, I don't think it matters, but we say we simply want it for information because obviously if we know they have been approached by the Defence, we want to make sure they understand they don't have to tell us anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the response of those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Lukic will get the full transcript and he -- they'll see exactly what the response was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean I'm not prepared to speculate without having the transcripts in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether those two witnesses would be treated as OTP witnesses or Defence witnesses? Do we have to have somebody present if we speak to them from the OTP office or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made this absolutely clear. If they were OTP witnesses they -- under Rule 66, the Defence would have been entitled to the full transcript and would have had it. We didn't -- we are not calling these witnesses because we do not regard them as witnesses who are anything other than hostile to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Already earlier, maybe it's the use of language you're acquainted with, but also taking into account the final result and the impression this Trial Chamber had, for example, by another witness where in anticipation of the hearing, the Prosecution tried to convince the Trial Chamber that this witness would be hostile or hostile to the Prosecution's case, I don't think this is the correct approach. Correct approach is that we have to hear witnesses as human beings, and especially under our mandate, under chapter 7, we have to be extremely careful to anticipate the evaluation of evidence and as experienced not only in our case but also in other cases show, they, as human beings, may decide to have another approach today to that what happened deplorably in 1992 and the following years in Former Yugoslavia. Therefore, both parties should not try, but unfortunately the common-law system is inviting for this, to see the witness of the respectively other side as a hostile one. I think we should not use this language. A witness is a witness, and we want to hear the testimony of these witnesses. And no doubt, it's for the Defence, if they so want, to summon these witnesses because in this case, no doubt, their testimony would be relevant. I wonder, having a view now to this entire motion of November 13, and having heard the explanations by the Prosecution and some remarks by the Trial Chamber, whether or not the Defence is upholding this entire motion? And then, please give some reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do uphold this motion. And I think that Mr. Ostojic gave all the reasons in the motion. And I think that they are fairly stated and clear and just. Also, I have to say that at the time when we gave our consent to continue with the trial, at that time we didn't know about those statements. And I have to say that at that time, we would surely advise our client differently than we did at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what is the prejudice you're suffering? As relates (c), you agreed that the access to the documents provided by the OTP suffices. As regards (d), the problem, I think, has been settled. And (e), this general clause that "further relief the Trial Chamber deems to be just and equitable" this also runs moot after we had settled (c) and (d). As regards (b), it's, as it stands here, and as you couldn't submit anything in addition to this, I can't see really any kind of prejudice. You yourself mention only certain witnesses, and maybe it's related to those witnesses mentioned in paragraph 31, 1 to 5. But where is the prejudice? Isn't it possible for the Defence, or alternatively, if the Defence tells us that there will be extreme difficulties to summon these witnesses and to bring them then to The Hague, I want to recall that this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, always has stated that in case the Defence feels it necessary that the Trial Chamber would issue an order of safe conduct if necessary; and in addition, if the situation in that area so allows, the Trial Chamber is prepared to hear a witness in Former Yugoslavia. So therefore, please tell us where is the problem, where you see the prejudice for your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I think that Your Honour remembers how many times you asked the witness who is to blame for everything that happened in the Prijedor area. I think that your question would be completely different and you could cross-examine differently every single witness you asked that question differently if you had those statements in front of you. Also, our position is that your decision based on Rule 98 bis would be different if you had these statements in front of you. So we think that the whole proceedings is impaired by not disclosing the statements which were available and taken before -- a few days before the trial. Those statements were not disclosed in a timely manner. Mentioning thousands of hours spent on 68 bis rule by the staff of the OTP, mentioning that this is not deliberately withheld is not true and cannot be applied to those statements because, as I said, they were taken a few days before the trial, taken by one of the OTP attorneys who is sitting in this trial. So obviously, those statements were deliberately withheld from the Chamber and from the Defence. And those statements would have huge impact on the whole case. So that's our position, and that's why at the first place we asked for the mistrial in this case and to have the trial from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do take grave exception on behalf of Mr. Koumjian who is perfectly able to speak for himself, to the allegations that I have lied or that Mr. Koumjian in some way has lied either to the Defence or to the Court. These interviews were conducted by Mr. Koumjian. They were on tape. They had to be transcribed, so the transcriptions were only available a short time, a shortish time again. That does not excuse, and I make no bones about it, my failure to order that the interviews should be searched for any Rule 68 material. Some of it was done and disclosed immediately. The fuller searches, and it is no good the Defence trying to avoid this, were not done because of the Defence declining to give us any assistance as to what the full nature of their case was. And so we had to do the searches on everything. We should have -- and I have said it over and over again, we should have started with those interviews. We didn't. That's our error. But if we were deliberately withholding, then why would we disclose at this stage, and thereby give the Defence the opportunity to put in the motion in the terms in which they did. But I deeply, deeply resent the allegation that Mr. Lukic makes with no foundation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to respond why did you disclose this? Because we approached one of these witnesses we didn't approach before, and probably he informed you because when he told us that he has been interviewed by the OTP, we immediately quit questioning him. And that's why you disclosed this, because you were informed that we were informed that that person gave you a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's pure speculation and wrong speculation. Not one of these witnesses has informed us that they were approached by the Defence. And as I say, what Mr. Lukic has just said exactly shows the situation that they knew who these witnesses were, they could have interviewed them at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't continue to discuss on guilt or not guilt on the one or other side. And it's not for the Trial Chamber to decide on this right now. I understand that from the motion of the Defence, provisionally filed the 13th of October, 2002, the official version I just learned from the registry is from 15 November, 2002, the accused Milomir Stakic's motion for mistrial, we have resolved points (b) to (e). And it's remaining point (a). And as I understood the Defence correctly, they desire a decision on this point (e) only after we have read the entire statements provided in disclosures 1163 ongoing. Is this correct, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the Trial Chamber will decide on this in due time. But, of course, not earlier than we have received the other documents in the moment the Trial Chamber having discussed this issue in advance before entering the courtroom, we didn't find any reason to intervene immediately. Let us now turn to the motion or the brief under 65 ter (g). And with some serious concern, we saw that, first of all, the first list, provisional list of witnesses, did not live up to the expectations provided for in the rules, in 65 ter (g). Leaving for a moment aside the question of the list of exhibits. But as for the witnesses, I have a lot of problems. Let's start with a more simple question: You have provided summaries for eight witnesses. Can we expect that it is planned to hear these witnesses during this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first witness will appear when?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have prepared, proofed, witnesses how many for today, one or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And his or her name, if not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the protective measures of this witness. It's male, so I thought it not necessary, but because of certain circumstances I would like to address in private session that I ask for some protective measures for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This question was only related to the question that we, in fact, can hear the witness today because one thing has to be said before going into details. To a certain extent, the submission of the Prosecution as to the relevance of these witnesses is correct in the closer sense of the word "relevance." And I think it's also necessary that we use in common a language the accused understands, not only related to the translation from English to B/C/S, but also to our legal language. When we use the term "relevant" or "irrelevant," that is related to our case before us only. Nobody could say that the testimony, prepared some extremely short summaries, but we know what the witnesses will testify about. Nobody could state that this what happened to these persons is irrelevant in a broader sense, irrelevant for the evaluation of what has happened in the territory of Former Yugoslavia since 1991. It is of importance. But we have to limit ourselves and our case for that -- to that what is really relevant for the decision in the concrete case. And here, we have to re-emphasise what we did in the beginning, that tu quoque is no defence. That means that the fact that other crimes have been no doubt committed on the territory of Former Yugoslavia as such is no defence. And therefore, and only therefore, one can speak about, as the OTP to a certain extent correctly did, state that the witness of the one or other -- the testimony of the one or other witness is not relevant in this sense. We don't want to go so far and state that the summoning of these witnesses for the first week could be seen as a kind of abuse of the more generous approach of this Trial Chamber not going into details of each and any witness in the framework of a pre-Defence conference. But apparently leaving it for you to summon the witnesses for the first week. The Trial Chamber decided not to reject and not to strike the witnesses from the list of witnesses because to a certain extent, it cannot totally be excluded that there is some relevance. Some relevance may be for the state of mind Dr. Stakic acted from the period of time envisaged in the fourth amended indictment. This is from April 1992 onwards. And as we understand, the witnesses will testify on that what happened immediately before. And there could be and there might be some relevance as regards if it would come, if I emphasise this, to a conviction, this could be regarded in a way as a mitigating factor. But primarily, the Trial Chamber will not give any assistance to the impression that this Tribunal is one-sided and only hearing witnesses from one side by sending back witnesses you have already summoned and giving them the impression that for this Tribunal, their testimony is not relevant. This would be a totally wrong impression, and therefore you may continue with these witnesses. And may I ask the period of time you need for the witnesses for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First for today, and then for the other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you, Your Honours, not to reject these witnesses. But also, I would like to emphasise that I learned a long time ago that tu quoque is not an admissible defence in front of this Tribunal. But the purpose of these witnesses is not tu quoque, the purpose of these witnesses as a core, an essence of this case, because the theory of the Prosecution is the Serbs had planned, the Serbs started everything. Through these witnesses we would show the Trial Chamber that the war hasn't been started by the Serbs, that the war was started by the invasion of Croatian regular troops into Bosnia. And that's not the defence as you mentioned, tu quoque. But we also know that the Prosecution does not claim that Dr. Stakic killed, mistreated, or did anything personally to anybody else. This case is a political case in which they try to show that there was a criminal plan. We have to show in any way that there is first that there is no criminal plan at all. Secondly, that Dr. Stakic is not part of that criminal plan. So if we want to show that there is no criminal plan, we have to start from somewhere. And we have decided to start from Bosanski Brod from the 3rd of March, 1992. Because it was a very well covered event in all Former Yugoslavia media. So it's not something which was isolated. And once again, I want to thank you for the opportunity to have these witnesses. And I estimate that if my opening statement would be short, I hope that we might finish the first witness today because it's the longest one. All other witnesses would be shorter, and I'll be able to finish them hopefully -- I tried to clarify actually today whether we work on Thursday or not. So it would help me also to plan. Because I have two schedules. In one Thursday is a working day; and the other one, we are not working on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say something before we carry on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One moment, please. There's no doubt at all that we will hear this case the entire week, and we have to go into all the details of your filing, especially the final list of witnesses. And we have to go through witness by witness. So therefore, no doubt, we will do the necessary -- what is necessary in a pre-Defence conference. But in order to take care of the witnesses, to take care that the witnesses do not come in vain and they are able to return to their home countries as soon as possible, the Trial Chamber is prepared to discuss the other witnesses not to be heard during this week, to discuss these issues later and not today. But I have to tell the Defence that we warned the Defence that their filings were not in compliance with that what can be expected under Rule 65 ter (g), and we mentioned that there could be some consequences related to 65 ter (n), or other adequate measures mentioned in this decision. And we have to come back to this, and we have to go through both briefs under 65 ter (g). But what I want to avoid is that the witnesses are waiting here whilst we are discussing these issues. Maybe later, but no doubt, we'll hear the case also on Thursday. Please, you were the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour didn't give me a chance before ruling to expand on our objection, but I think I ought to say this. Your Honour is concerned that witnesses would come here that nobody wants to hear their story. Your Honour, there are cases preceding in this Tribunal prosecuting Croats, prosecuting Muslims. Your Honours, those witnesses could have submitted their testimony or could have been sought in those cases. Your Honours, this is nothing more than a tu quoque Defence, and we don't dispute it. Your Honour, we don't dispute that the Croats in some places behaved as badly as the Serbs. There's a case that's just finished in relation to that. We don't dispute that Muslims behaved badly, and we do not see how a witness from Bosanski Brod can assist Your Honours to arrive at a decision relating to the events in Prijedor and Dr. Stakic's part in them. Your Honour, I've heard your ruling, but I just want to make that absolutely clear that Your Honours having stopped us from going outside the Prijedor region or any part of our evidence, Your Honours we hope that in a rebuttal case Your Honours will now extend us the same leniency and we can lead evidence from other municipalities as well, relevant we would say to the issue. Your Honour, that is not the main complaint at the moment. Your Honour, I don't know what witness has been called today. The summary, there's not a word about Bosanski Brod. I don't know which witness. The summaries are so wholly inadequate as to tell us anything about these witnesses. We have been wholly unable really to do any meaningful search on the information that has been supplied to us. If one takes the first witness, I don't know if that one who has been called at page 14315 of the filing, it appears to be a man who will speak about Croatian regular army troops that entered Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 3rd of March, 2002. I take it that's a typing error. But why, who, what, what town, what area, what events? It's an absolute disgrace --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I already mentioned that we have to go into the consequences of the omission by the Defence later on, and we still have not yet decided on the sanctions foreseen under 65 ter (n). My own concern is that maybe there are different glasses. There are hour glasses, and there are the glasses and the views taken by these witnesses coming here to The Hague. And this is only the point bringing the Trial Chamber to allow this, and I used deliberately the word "abuse" in the context of summoning this witness in -- earlier this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I'm asking is that we should now before any witness is called today, if Your Honour is going to adjourn consideration of this inadequate filing, that we now be told who the witness is, a proper summary of what the witness is going to say, in writing before this witness is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Being aware that we have to have our necessary break immediately, could we hear, what is the time frame you will need for the presentation of your case, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think a bit more than one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Could you then tell us, in fact, who will be the first witness and what period of time will it take? And maybe you have prepared a summary that you can read into the transcript right now, that we all, also the Judges sometimes want to prepare to decide on the relevance or not relevance of the one or other question, that we have this in preparation before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible to go to private session, Your Honour, because this should be a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.20.
